candidate.answerReason: Four socks may all have different colors, but five socks among four colors must include a matching pair.

methods.label: Consider the most socks without a match
methods.explanation:
It is possible to pull four socks with no matching pair by getting one of each color. Thus four socks do not guarantee a match.

With five socks, avoiding a match would require five different colors, but the drawer contains only four colors. Therefore any five socks include two of the same color. The minimum is \(\boxed{5}\), choice \(\text{C}\).
methods.levelReason: A direct comparison of five socks with four color categories proves the guarantee.

candidate.annotationRationale: The solution applies the basic pigeonhole principle and establishes minimality by exhibiting four unmatched socks. No quotient, remainder, or generalized occupancy formula is needed.

review.mathematicalCheck: One sock of each color gives four socks without a match, proving four insufficient. Five socks cannot all have different colors when only four colors exist, proving five sufficient.
review.levelCheck: The elementary argument clearly establishes both the guarantee and its minimality.
review.methodDistinctness: One direct pigeonhole argument is sufficient.
